newsitem.title: USA: Two dozen potential jurors sent home in Broin case.
newsitem.headline: Two dozen potential jurors sent home in Broin case.

text.p: The Florida judge in the Broin secondhand smoke trial on Monday dismissed as unacceptable a potential juror who compared suing tobacco companies for smoking-related illness to blaming high cholesterol on fast-food restaurants.

Dade County Circuit Court Robert Kaye dismissed the prospective juror at the end of the first day of selecting a jury to try the Broin lawsuit. It claims $5 billion in damages on allegations that cigarette makers are responsible for tobacco-related illness among some 60,000 flight attendants exposed to secondhand smoke on U.S. passenger flights.

Just five potential jurors, who may still be cut later in a winnowing expected to last all week or longer, survived from 29 considered on Monday by rival attorneys. The five include a smoker whose father died of a smoking-linked ailment and the daughter of a northern Florida tobacco farmer.
Nineteen other prospective jurors were scheduled to be questioned on Tuesday. Another 200 were on standby in the process of selecting six jurors and six to 12 alternates.

Under questioning by Stanley Rosenblatt, an attorney for the flight attendants, the woman later dismissed by Kaye said the causes of lung cancer and other tobacco-related diseases were hard to identify and that each smoker chose to accept the health risks of the practice.

A former smoker, the woman dueled with Rosenblatt on the issue of tobacco companies' legal liability for smoking illnesses. "You're saying that if I had high cholesterol, I should sue" fast-food restaurants, the ex-smoker said.
She also told Rosenblatt that the causes of the illnesses among the flight attendants, including lead plaintiff Norma Broin, were likely too many and varied to identify with any certainity.
"I don't know who to blame: the tobacco companies, the flight attendants or the air conditioning coming out of the vents," she said.
Rosenblatt said the woman was biased, and Kaye agreed over objections from tobacco-company lawyers.
Another juror candidate was sent home after he told the court his mother had wed her second husband at the home of one of the tobacco company lawyers.

Kaye earlier refused a request by another flight attendants attorney for the dismissal of two women in the pool of potential jurors. One of them said the ailing flight attendants should have found other work to avoid secondhand smoke, while the other wavered over whether she would be able to find the tobacco companies liable for the alleged injuries.
Lawyers on both sides have the right to refuse a limited number of potential jurors without explanation. Rosenblatt did not refuse either of the jurors but could do so later.

During the questioning, lawyers for both sides probed the potential jurors about their smoking habits and family medical histories connected to cigarettes. Jurors were also asked whether cigarettes and cigarette advertising should be banned in the United States and whether they could hear a trial expected to last two months or longer.
